sentences.text: Wapuskanectes is classified as a genus within the family Elasmosauridae, a group of long-necked marine reptiles.
The specific name 'nectes' in the genus name comes from the Greek word for 'swimmer'.
Gastroliths in one specimen were found poking out of the dorsal side between the ribs, indicating the animal rested on its back after death.
Despite being ten times heavier than the similar reptile Nichollsaura, Wapuskanectes carried gastroliths weighing five times as much.
The genus Wapuskanectes was named by Druckenmiller and Russell in 2006.

The holotype specimen of Wapuskanectes is an articulated partial postcranial skeleton that includes an almost complete pectoral girdle, collected from the western side of the Syncrude Base Mine near Fort McMurray.

Several specimens of Wapuskanectes have been discovered, with the most complete found 30 km away from the original mine site when heavy machinery ploughed through the fossil, destroying the skull and most of the neck.
The gastroliths found in Wapuskanectes have a composition similar to early Aptian conglomerate rocks from the Cadomin Formation.
Researchers hypothesize that Wapuskanectes swam westward to collect gastroliths from eroding beaches and river mouths along the western coast of the Western Interior Seaway.

Wapuskanectes is the oldest known elasmosaurid in North America, dating to approximately 112 million years ago during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous, between 113.2 and 110.1 million years ago.
Fossils of Wapuskanectes have been found in Alberta, Canada, within the Albian-aged Wabiskaw Member of the Clearwater Formation.
